subject: ✋ Slowing it down

Axios AI+
By Ina Fried and Madison Mills · Sep 14, 2026

Don't worry, the CEOs are going to slow down AI development. Problem solved!

  • And by solved, we mean nowhere near solved. Read on.

Today's AI+ is 1,397 words, a 5.5-minute read.

Situational awareness: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman tweeted last night that "pacing" AI development doesn't mean "stopping," saying development should follow a "narrow middle path."
 
 
1 big thing: Washington's AI paralysis
By Zachary Basu
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

President Trump is as all-in on AI as a politician could be: all gas, no brakes, and zero interest in hand-wringing about dystopian risks or public disdain.

  • Democrats are as conflicted on AI as a party could be: skeptical of the labs, spooked by their warnings, but split on whether to shut it all down.

Why it matters: This staggering divide makes consensus on federal AI regulation almost unimaginable this year — and probably through early 2029, regardless of who wins control of Congress.

Zoom in: Trump has governed as the AI president from Day 1, applying the same doctrine to models and the data centers that power them — build faster, regulate less, beat China.

  • Speaking in Ireland yesterday, he dismissed new safety warnings as the work of "a lot of negative forces ... bringing up things that won't happen" — and reduced the stakes to one line: "Whoever wins AI wins."
  • It's unclear which "negative forces" Trump has in mind: Calls to slow the race — or "pace the frontier" — are now coming from the leaders of America's premier AI labs, including Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google.

Between the lines: Trump's accelerationist allies, including venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, see the safety alarms as a cynical ploy by the field's dominant players to lock in favorable regulations.

  • David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar and a leading voice for the administration's hands-off approach, has a simple answer: Slow yourselves down.
  • If OpenAI and Anthropic truly think the frontier is moving too fast, Sacks argues, they can decelerate on their own without using Washington to force competitors to do the same.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) echoed Sacks' argument that the labs don't need Congress to slow themselves down — and rejected calls for an emergency moratorium.

  • Johnson said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he'd recall the House and put AI regulation to a vote "if we had the solution," but warned Congress against rushing into rules it doesn't yet understand.
  • His preferred first step is a summit: Johnson said yesterday he wants Trump, congressional leaders and the heads of the major AI labs in a room as soon as possible to hammer out a common approach to safety.

The other side: Congressional Democrats are coalescing around urgency but have no comparable doctrine on what to actually do.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says his caucus will meet tomorrow to debate what action to take, while former President Barack Obama is privately urging the party to make AI a top priority.

The policy spectrum is vast — and doesn't neatly map onto what the labs themselves are asking for.

  • On the progressive end, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) want to ban superintelligence outright, pause advanced AI development and threaten violators with up to 20 years in prison.
  • Others are reaching for more conventional Washington fixes: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) wants a bipartisan AI select committee with subpoena power, while Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is demanding that OpenAI open its models to federal safety reviews.

2. Scoop: Coxon, Bernie and Bannon unite
By Maria Curi
 

Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call Inc. via Getty Images
 

Ex-Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and former Trump White House adviser Steve Bannon will join forces at an event tomorrow to push for human-controlled AI.

Why it matters: An industry insider, the face of the progressive movement and a leading MAGA voice make for unlikely allies, in a sign of how AI is upending political norms.

Driving the news: The Future of Life Institute is organizing tomorrow's "Pro-Human Assembly." The nonprofit advocacy group is behind the "Pro-Human AI Declaration," which calls for protecting human agency, avoiding concentrations of power and holding companies accountable.

  • Coxon, who worked for OpenAI and then Anthropic and quit the latter over safety fears, will give in-person remarks, Axios has learned.
  • "The Oligarchs are finally being forced to admit they've lied from the beginning about the dangers of acceleration with zero guardrails — they've put the nation and mankind in jeopardy," Bannon told Axios in a statement.

The intrigue: The event will showcase officials from across the political spectrum and span viewpoints from Hollywood to faith groups.

3. Microsoft: "People matter more than AI"
By Ina Fried
 

Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Penguin Random House
 

Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman says the race to build ever more powerful AI needs a red line: AI must remain under human control.

Why it matters: Microsoft is taking a harder line than rivals on AI design when there is growing concern that the industry's current path could threaten humanity.

What they're saying: That could mean sacrificing capabilities others are willing to pursue.

  • "I think some people think that it's inevitable that superintelligence is going to exceed human control," Suleyman told Axios.
  • "But I don't agree with that. I think that would be very, very dangerous, and it means that we're going to have to make decisions about what we're not going to do."

Driving the news: Microsoft today published a new "Humanist AI" code of conduct that says people must retain meaningful control.

  • The code says Microsoft AI models should remain subordinate to humans and rejects "the race to produce an all-purpose superintelligence."
  • Microsoft says it is willing to compromise on "ultimate generality, autonomy, or capability" to preserve safety and control, and models should never resist human input, nor should they set their own goals.
  • Microsoft also says AI should be designed as a tool rather than a person, and AI should increase human agency rather than foster dependence.
  • There's a lot more in the 9,000-word document, but Microsoft says it really can be boiled down to these five words: "People matter more than AI."

4. The scramble to build AI kill switches
By Herb Scribner
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

AI companies are already building emergency brakes to stop nefarious AI systems before they cause serious damage and kill us all.

OpenAI overhauled its response system following the Hugging Face incident.

  • According to the company, an AI security guard monitoring AI chain-of-thought will alert staffers when an agent appears to be doing something dangerous.
  • Responders are then charged with pausing activity unless they identify it as a false alarm within 30 minutes.

Anthropic's strategy involves using AI to monitor AI. In a report on Claude Opus 4.6 risk, Anthropic said it had automated monitoring to identify sabotage and misbehavior.

  • The monitoring caught 50% of malicious behavior, the company says.

Salesforce's MuleSoft developed an actual product called "Agent Kill Switch," which targets the resources AI agents need to live.

  • An operator can halt a single request, session, agent, or — in an emergency — an entire company account.

5. AI debt surges — and gets more complicated
By Emily Peck
 
Note: S&P Global adjusted debt metric accounts for items including company cash holdings and the value of future lease obligations and power purchase agreements. Data: S&P Global; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

AI financing is getting bigger and more complicated, and the pristine credit ratings of the Big Tech hyperscalers are at risk, warns S&P.

Why it matters: The trillions these companies are spending — much of it borrowed — to fund data centers and other AI-related infrastructure are fueling U.S. economic growth overall.

What they're saying: "The credit quality of hyperscalers is gradually weakening," the S&P analysts wrote.

  • They forecast that the top six hyperscalers — Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Oracle, SpaceX and Meta — will spend more than $7 trillion on data centers and AI capex through 2030.

The big picture: The issue is that these established players are lending their reputations and credit ratings to smaller and untested companies — neoclouds, data center operators and unproven yet giant startups like Anthropic and OpenAI.

  • "When we get together and talk about where the risks are from AI, it's these smaller companies," said Naveen Sarma, an analyst at S&P who coauthored the report.

Full story.
 
 
6. Training data
 
  • Chinese President Xi Jinping says China will lead the way on AI cooperation and development among developing countries. (CNBC)
  • It's very difficult to have a sober conversation about AI risk when there's so much money at stake, Dan Primack writes. (Axios)
  • Inference chip startup Positron AI raised $500 million at a $5 billion valuation just one month after closing $375 million at a $3.9 billion valuation. (Axios Pro Deals)
  • Climate tech company Tomorrow.io is building a new generation of weather satellites that could give billions of people earlier warnings about dangerous storms. (Axios)
